extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, policymakers, and aviation/transportation professionals interested in airline incidents and policy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing the April 9, 2017 United Express Flight 3411 passenger removal, including chronology, investigations, legal/regulatory issues, airline and government responses, and public relations consequences. Useful as a case study for airline policy, use-of-force, passenger rights, and crisis communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Force Policy (Chicago Department of Aviation)
rubrics_metrics.description: OIG: 'Specifically, the first ASO violated the CDA Use of Force Policy when that ASO escalated a non-threatening situation into a physically violent one by forcefully removing a passenger from the aircraft.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use-of-force rules require officers not to escalate non-threatening situations into physical violence; force must be proportionate and in accordance with department policy. The OIG finding describes concrete consequences when policy is violated (injuries, disciplinary actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and completeness of official incident reports
rubrics_metrics.description: OIG found the second ASO 'made misleading statements in two reports' and the third ASO 'made material omissions in a report', and that the Sergeant 'deliberately removed material facts from the third ASO's "To/From Report" and approved reports without all essential information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incident documentation must be truthful, complete, and include all essential information; supervisors must not alter or remove material facts. Misleading statements or omissions can form independent violations and lead to disciplinary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and legal classification of airport security personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chicago Department of Aviation Security officers' powers differ from those of the Chicago Police Department; for example, its officers cannot file arrest reports. The Illinois Law Enforcement Training and Standards Board decertified the Chicago Department of Aviation Police, stating the agency is 'in no way' a police agency, merely a security force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and personnel must be correctly classified under law and properly authorized for the actions they take. Improper labeling (e.g., calling security 'police') or acting beyond statutory authority creates legal and oversight problems and may prompt decertification or changes in response protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with denied boarding / oversales regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: USDOT: 'While it is legal for airlines to [involuntarily] bump passengers from an oversold flight when there are not enough volunteers, it is the airline's responsibility to determine its own fair boarding priorities.' John Banzhaf: United was 'citing the wrong federal rule to justify its illegal request to force a passenger already boarded and seated to disembark, since the regulation cited only covers denial of boarding, and not removing a passenger after boarding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Airlines must apply the correct federal rules (denied boarding/oversales) and ensure actions taken after boarding are authorized by regulation and the carrier's contract of carriage. Citing the wrong rule may render an action unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on involuntary removal after check-in/boarding (USDOT rule change)
rubrics_metrics.description: On January 13, 2021, the USDOT amended its rules, effective April 2021, to require that 'a passenger may not be denied permission to board or be involuntarily removed from an airliner once they have checked in for the flight prior to the deadline and had their ticket or boarding pass collected or electronically scanned and accepted by the gate agent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory protection now bars involuntary removal after check-in/boarding-pass acceptance; airlines must adjust policies and procedures to comply, affecting how carriers handle 'must-ride' employees and oversold situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to airline Contract of Carriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party legal commentary: 'While United has asserted a right to remove passengers after boarding, none of the reasons for doing so specified in the airline's contract of carriage applied in this situation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Airlines must act within the rights and procedures set out in their contract of carriage; removing a passenger for reasons not covered risks legal liability and breach-of-contract claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of law enforcement/security for passenger removal
rubrics_metrics.description: United announced it would no longer use police in involuntary bumping situations: 'We're not going to put a law enforcement official ... [onto a United aircraft] to remove a booked, paid, seated passenger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice emerging from the incident: avoid deploying police or security officers to remove paying, seated passengers except in genuine safety or criminal situations. Airlines should have internal procedures and escalation policies that minimize law-enforcement involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communication: timeliness and tone of corporate statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of United CEO Oscar Munoz: initial statement used 're-accommodating' and defended crew, which was widely ridiculed; PRWeek and others called his handling a 'fumbling response' and an example of how not to respond in a crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective crisis communication should be timely, genuinely apologetic when appropriate, avoid minimizing language or corporate euphemisms, avoid prematurely defending staff, take responsibility, promise corrective action, and follow up with substantive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer and compensation policies for voluntary bumps
rubrics_metrics.description: Passengers were initially offered $400 vouchers then $800 to voluntarily give up seats; in response to the incident United later raised maximum amounts up to $10,000, and other carriers increased amounts (e.g., Delta's increase and Southwest's decision to stop overbooking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation levels and the process for recruiting volunteers can reduce the need for involuntary removals; transparent, generous, and well-communicated offers are part of fair boarding practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew-travel/booking policies to avoid displacing passengers
rubrics_metrics.description: United internally announced a policy change to ensure that flight crews are booked 'at least 60 minutes prior to departure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational policies that ensure crew 'must-ride' allocations are resolved well before boarding can prevent last-minute displacement of paying customers; scheduling practices should minimize risk of conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary and accountability measures following investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to the OIG report the CDA discharged James Long and John Moore and issued five-day suspensions to Rodriguez and Smith; the OIG established violations of personnel rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should lead to appropriate accountability (discharge, suspension, retraining) where personnel violated policy. Transparent reporting of disciplinary outcomes supports public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of evidence for litigation and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Dao's lawyer asked for an order requiring United and the city of Chicago to retain all video, cockpit recordings, and other reports from the flight, including personnel files of the Aviation Department officers; United and the city agreed, forgoing a court hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations involved in incidents must preserve relevant evidence (video, recordings, personnel files, reports) to comply with legal obligations and oversight inquiries; failure to preserve can lead to sanctions and undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and regulatory remedies to protect passengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional and state responses included bills (e.g., Customers Not Cargo Act, Airline Passenger Protection Act) and eventual USDOT/14 CFR amendments that changed boarding and removal rules; Illinois introduced the Airline Passenger Protection Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When industry practices are seen as inadequate, legislative or regulatory change can establish new mandatory protections (e.g., banning involuntary removal after boarding/check-in), requiring carriers and airports to change policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accuracy in initial public statements
rubrics_metrics.description: United initially said Flight 3411 was 'overbooked' and later 'clarified' that the flight was not overbooked but sold out and the four employees were 'must-ride' passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations should ensure initial public statements are accurate; inconsistent or misleading early statements can exacerbate public outrage and harm credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation between oversold flights and accommodating employees ('must-ride')
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions were raised whether bumping passengers to accommodate employees is the same as an 'oversold' situation; United at one point stated the four employees were 'must-ride' passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should clearly state how carrier prioritizes boarding when accommodating employees versus volunteers, and explain how these situations relate to oversales rules to avoid misapplication of denied-boarding procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passenger rights to compensation and legal remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Passengers affected by involuntary denied boarding or forcible removal may seek compensation; Dao filed suit and later reached a confidential settlement. USDOT and later laws provide protections and guidelines for denied boarding compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passengers retain statutory and contractual rights; carriers should provide clear information about compensation entitlements and legal remedies, and consider fair settlements where harm occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational and insignia/branding accuracy for security units
rubrics_metrics.description: Following review, the Chicago Department of Aviation reported that its unsworn, unarmed airport security personnel were not actually police officers under Illinois law; their uniforms, badges and vehicles had been 'improperly' labeled 'police' for historical reasons and the incorrect insignia would be removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should ensure that uniforms, badges, vehicles, and titles accurately reflect legal authority to prevent public confusion about the role and powers of security personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of social media and media coverage in shaping responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Video footage recorded by passengers went viral, resulting in anger and calls for investigation; social media mobilization led to petitions and calls for boycotts, and the incident trended internationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations must anticipate rapid amplification via social media; crisis response should include monitoring, rapid factual corrections, empathetic messaging, and substantive policy responses to mitigate reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight and reporting obligations to Congress and regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Bipartisan senators and congressional committees sought information from United and the Chicago Department of Aviation; USDOT reviewed the incident to determine whether the airline complied with the oversales rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carriers and airport authorities should be prepared to provide timely, complete responses to oversight bodies and regulators; cooperation and transparency are critical in inquiries.
